common_name: Wizard Scarlet Coleus (Compact Bright Red Seed-Grown Coleus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant after all frost danger has passed; Wizard Scarlet is a compact, seed-grown Wizard series coleus with bright red, slightly ruffled leaves edged in green, tolerant of both sun and shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Wizard Scarlet bears bright, slightly ruffled red leaves edged in a contrasting green margin on a compact, uniform, seed-grown plant bred for reliable garden performance from a young age. Its small stature and adaptability to a wide range of light conditions make it a versatile choice for edging, mass bedding, and containers where a compact, colorful foliage plant is wanted. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sun and Shade Coleus Selection

common_name: Wizard Mosaic Coleus (Green Foliage Speckled with Red Mottling)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant after all frost danger has passed; Wizard Mosaic is a compact, seed-grown coleus with bright green leaves speckled and splotched with red in a mottled mosaic pattern.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Wizard Mosaic bears bright green leaves irregularly speckled and blotched with red in a distinctive mottled pattern that gives each leaf a unique, mosaic-like appearance, distinguishing it from solid-colored coleus cultivars. Its compact, uniform, heat-tolerant habit and tolerance of both sun and shade make it a versatile choice for edging, mass bedding, and containers. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller, more colorful foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sun and Shade Coleus Selection

common_name: Kong Red Coleus (Giant Dark Burgundy Shade Coleus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant container plants after the last frost in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kong Red bears huge, palm-sized dark burgundy leaves with scarlet ribs and irregular green margins, needing protection from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and keep soil consistently moist, since the Kong series' enormous leaves wilt quickly in dry conditions. Kong Red bears exceptionally large, heart-shaped leaves in dark burgundy with vivid scarlet ribs and an irregular green margin, among the boldest color combinations in the Kong series bred specifically for large-leaved shade performance. Its dramatic size and rich color make a striking textural statement massed in a shaded bed or as a specimen in a large container, pairing well with ferns, hostas, and other big-leaved shade perennials. Pinch flower spikes as they appear to keep energy directed into leaf growth, and pinch growing tips periodically for a fuller habit.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Kong coleus series notes

common_name: Velvet Mocha Coleus (Rich Mocha-Maroon Sun Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Velvet Mocha, part of the ColorBlaze series, bears rich, solid mocha-maroon foliage bred for heat tolerance and minimal flowering, so the color show lasts all season.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Velvet Mocha, part of the ColorBlaze series bred specifically for full-sun garden performance, bears rich, velvety mocha-maroon foliage with almost no pattern or variegation, giving it a deep, uniform color that reads almost solid from a distance and pairs well as a dark foil for brighter companion plants. Like other ColorBlaze selections it flowers very late in the season, so the foliage display continues largely uninterrupted through summer without frequent pinching. Water regularly during establishment and pinch growing tips occasionally to maintain a full, bushy habit.
sources: Proven Winners — ColorBlaze coleus series notes

common_name: Chocolate Drop Coleus (Compact Deep Chocolate-Maroon Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Chocolate Drop is a compact ColorBlaze series coleus with small, deep chocolate-maroon leaves on a dense, mounding plant well suited to containers.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Chocolate Drop stays notably compact for a ColorBlaze series coleus, bearing small, deep chocolate-maroon leaves on a dense, tightly mounding plant that fits containers, edging, and small-scale plantings where larger coleus cultivars would sprawl. Its rich, dark, near-solid coloring provides a strong contrast foil for brighter flowers and foliage nearby. Water regularly during establishment and pinch growing tips occasionally to maintain a full, bushy habit; flowers late in the season like other ColorBlaze selections.
sources: Proven Winners — ColorBlaze coleus series notes

common_name: Habanero Coleus (Narrow Ruffled Spicy-Orange Sun Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Habanero, part of the FlameThrower series, bears narrow, ruffled, spicy-orange foliage on a plant bred for full sun to part shade and very late flowering.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; the FlameThrower series was bred specifically for strong sun tolerance. Habanero bears narrow, deeply ruffled, fiery orange leaves that live up to the series' spicy naming theme, forming an upright, well-branched plant that holds its vivid color through summer heat better than many older coleus cultivars. Like other FlameThrower selections it flowers very late in the season, keeping the foliage display uninterrupted for months. Water regularly during establishment and pinch growing tips occasionally to maintain a full, bushy habit.
sources: Proven Winners — FlameThrower coleus series notes

common_name: Chili Pepper Coleus (Narrow Serrated Burgundy-and-Lime Sun Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Chili Pepper, part of the FlameThrower series, bears narrow, serrated leaves variegated dark burgundy and lime green, bred for full sun to part shade and very late flowering.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; the FlameThrower series was bred specifically for strong sun tolerance. Chili Pepper bears narrow, finely serrated leaves splashed with dark burgundy and lime green in a striking bicolor pattern, forming an upright, well-branched plant that holds its vivid color through summer heat better than many older coleus cultivars. Like other FlameThrower selections it flowers very late in the season, keeping the foliage display uninterrupted for months. Water regularly during establishment and pinch growing tips occasionally to maintain a full, bushy habit.
sources: Proven Winners — FlameThrower coleus series notes

common_name: Trusty Rusty Coleus (Award-Winning Rust-and-Magenta Gold-Edged Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Trusty Rusty is an RHS Award of Garden Merit winner with large rust-and-magenta leaves edged golden-yellow, tolerant of both sun and part shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Trusty Rusty, a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit winner, bears large leaves in warm rust and magenta tones edged with a bright golden-yellow margin, a rich, warm color combination that has made it a standout in trial gardens. Its adaptability to a range of light conditions and strong garden performance suit it to mixed borders, containers, and mass plantings alike. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Award of Garden Merit

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Sedona Sunset bears soft coppery-orange foliage that intensifies in color with more sun exposure, adaptable to sun or shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Sedona Sunset bears soft, warm coppery-orange leaves that deepen and intensify in color with increasing sun exposure, giving gardeners flexibility to grow it in a range of light conditions while still getting strong color, unlike many coleus cultivars that fade or scorch in full sun. Its large, vigorous, well-branched habit makes a bold statement in a mixed border or large container. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.
sources: Proven Winners — ColorBlaze coleus series notes

common_name: Bone Fish Coleus (Narrow Deeply Lobed Fuchsia-Pink Coleus)
scientific_name: Coleus scutellarioides 'Under the Sea Bone Fish'

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Bone Fish, part of the Under the Sea series, bears narrow, deeply lobed fuchsia-pink leaves edged gold to pale green, a fine, delicate texture unlike typical broad-leaved coleus.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Bone Fish, part of the distinctively fine-textured Under the Sea coleus series, bears narrow, deeply lobed leaves in vivid fuchsia-pink edged with gold fading to pale green, a delicate, feathery look that sets it apart from the broad, solid leaves of typical coleus cultivars and adds fine textural contrast in a mixed planting. Its unusual leaf shape and bright color work well in containers and at the front of a border. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into fuller foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.
sources: Proven Winners — Under the Sea coleus series notes

common_name: Cherry Choco Latte Hibiscus (White with Pink Veining and Chocolate Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Cherry Choco Latte is a Summerific series cultivar with huge white flowers veined deep pink around a large red eye, over dark chocolate-tinged foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Cherry Choco Latte bears enormous, 8-9 inch white flowers intricately veined in deep pink radiating from a large red eye, held against dark, chocolate-tinged foliage that adds moody contrast beneath the pale blooms. It flowers in a steady succession of huge blooms from midsummer into fall, each lasting a single day but replaced continuously by new buds. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown, and watch for Japanese beetle damage on foliage and flowers where present.

common_name: Southern Belle Hibiscus (Classic Mixed-Color Seed-Strain Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container plants or start seed indoors in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Southern Belle is a classic seed-strain giving mixed white, pink, and red 10-inch blooms on a tall, four-to-six-foot plant.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, providing consistent water throughout the growing season since hardy hibiscus is naturally a wetland-edge plant. Southern Belle is a classic, long-cultivated seed strain producing enormous, 10-inch dinner-plate flowers in a mix of white, pink, and red on the same planting, giving a colorful, varied display on tall, robust, four-to-six-foot plants. Its seed-grown, mixed-color nature makes it economical for filling a large area with bold summer color. Like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location, and watch for Japanese beetle damage where present.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Hardy Hibiscus Cultivars
